extracted.intended_audience: IP attorneys, in-house counsel, and practitioners handling design patents
extracted.subtask_short: design patent infringement and validity standards
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards and practical guidance for assessing design patent infringement, anticipation/validity, obviousness, and treatment of functional elements following Egyptian Goddess; also outlines a proposed statutory regime for fashion-design protection. Intended to guide practitioners on applicable tests, evidentiary focuses, and procedural questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary Observer test for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is found when the accused design is substantially similar to the patented design as determined by the ordinary observer; the focus is on the overall appearance of the accused and patented designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific features or points of novelty are no longer the proper bases for comparison; the Federal Circuit in Egyptian Goddess eliminated the separate 'point of novelty' requirement and re-established the 'ordinary observer' test as the sole criterion for literal infringement. Evaluate the overall visual impression rather than isolated ornamental aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of novelty test eliminated
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holders no longer need to show that the accused device 'appropriated the novelty in the patented device which distinguishes from the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously a two-pronged test required both the point of novelty test and the ordinary observer test; Egyptian Goddess removed the point of novelty prong, so infringement analysis should not hinge on proving appropriation of particular novel features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary Observer test for anticipation/validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation (invalidity for lack of novelty) in design patent cases occurs if the ordinary observer determines that the patented design is substantially similar to cited prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International Seaway Trading Corp. v. Walgreens Corp. holds that because the ordinary observer test is the correct standard for infringement, it is likewise the correct standard for comparing a patented design to the prior art when assessing anticipation. Use overall visual similarity to prior art rather than point-by-point feature comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard for design patents (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness in design patent cases is assessed using the standard four-part framework: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) level of ordinary skill in the art; (3) differences between the prior art and the claimed design; and (4) objective indicia of non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Crocs v. ITC, the Federal Circuit applied these factors and reversed a finding of obviousness where (a) claimed features were missing from the cited prior art, (b) an ordinary artisan would not have been motivated to add the missing elements, and (c) the accused product had significant commercial success—illustrating the types of evidence that can rebut obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary considerations to defeat an obviousness finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that can defeat an obviousness finding includes demonstrable absence of claimed features in the prior art, lack of a motivation to combine or modify prior art to reach the claimed design, and strong objective indicia such as commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crocs v. ITC exemplifies relying on (a) showing one or more claimed features are missing from cited prior art, (b) arguing an ordinary artisan would not be motivated to add missing elements, and (c) presenting substantial commercial success as objective indicia of non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of functional elements in design patent analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional elements of a design should be ignored when undertaking the infringement/validity analysis; the deception must arise from the overall design, not from similarities in ornamental features in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richardson v. Stanley Works instructs that the deception leading to infringement must result from the overall design. When comparing designs, discount functional aspects and focus on ornamental/visual aspects. It remains an open question whether this analysis is a matter for a Markman claim-construction hearing or for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of claim construction (Markman) vs. jury in design comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclear whether analysis of which elements to ignore (e.g., functional elements) and related interpretive matters belong to a Markman claim-construction hearing or should be left to the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be mindful of this unresolved procedural question when planning litigation strategy—be prepared to address both claim-construction arguments and jury-focused presentation of overall-appearance comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of design patents by industry/product lifecycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents are especially useful in industries and product categories with longer product life cycles (consumer goods, tools, jewelry), and less obviously suited to industries with very short lifecycles such as fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because design patents provide limited-duration protection and require enforcement, they tend to be more practical where products have enduring sales and where the administrative/enforcement costs can be justified. For fashion, alternative or legislative fixes have been proposed to address rapid-cycle copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative Design Protection and Piracy Prevention Act — subject matter and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed S.3728 would create a special form of design protection (by amending copyright law) for fashion and fashion-related items, providing three years of protection for qualifying works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to categories such as clothing, wallets, handbags, belts, suitcases, and eyeglass frames. Duration under the bill (as of this bulletin) is three years of protection for qualifying works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative Design Protection and Piracy Prevention Act — eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the proposed bill, a fashion-related work would be protected if (a) it is the result of the designer's own creative endeavor, and (b) it provides a unique non-utilitarian variation over prior designs for the same article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill frames eligibility in terms of authorship/creativity and a non-utilitarian (ornamental) novelty requirement relative to prior designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative Design Protection and Piracy Prevention Act — infringement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement under the proposed legislation would require actual copying and that the resulting work be 'substantially identical in overall visual appearance' as to the original elements of the protected design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill's infringement test emphasizes proof of copying and substantial identity of overall visual appearance (mirroring the ordinary-observer focus) rather than independent design or minor differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative Design Protection and Piracy Prevention Act — registration and pleading changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed legislation would remove the registration requirement for pursuing an infringement claim and would substitute a more detailed pleading requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, this would lower a formal barrier (registration) but raise initial pleading detail obligations; practitioners should watch for how this affects early-stage litigation and enforcement strategies in the fashion context.
